title: Two distances: where are you?
hook: Your phone knows how far you are from two cities. Is that enough to find you?

knows: a phone can find its position from satellites
doesNotKnow: why one or two distances are not enough
that each distance is a circle

misconception: Two known distances from two known points pin you to one place.
objective: The learner can say that each known distance is a circle, that two circles cross in two places, and that a third distance picks one of them.

claims.text: Each distance alone puts you somewhere on a circle, and two circles cross twice.
claims.source: Small-circle intersection on a sphere (any spherical trigonometry text); the stage computes the crossings by vector algebra with the radii it draws. At Paris 1,000 km and Rome 800 km there are two crossings; at 600/400 km there are none (node, builder's scratch script; also none at 300/400 and 200/200).

claims.text: One crossing is over Austria and the other is in the Mediterranean near the Balearic Islands.
claims.source: Node: crossings at 16.01 E 48.66 N (geoContains on the lesson's 1:110m countries: Austria) and 3.35 E 39.89 N (in no country polygon; the 1:110m data has no Balearic Islands, so 'near the Balearic Islands' is the builder's reading of the coordinates from memory of the map). City coordinates from a gazetteer, from memory: Paris 48.8566 N 2.3522 E, Rome 41.9028 N 12.4964 E, Madrid 40.4168 N 3.7038 W.

claims.text: A third distance, 602 km from Madrid, fits only the sea crossing; the Austrian crossing is 1,804 km from Madrid.
claims.source: Node on a sphere of R = 6,371.0088 km: Madrid to the sea crossing 602.3 km, to the Austrian crossing 1,803.7 km. (The brief's figures, 810 km and 2,280 km, did not reproduce with these coordinates; the stage uses the computed 602 km, derived in the code from the same crossings.)

claims.text: Position fixing works by circles: each distance is a circle and a further circle removes the extra crossing. Satellite positioning uses the same idea in three dimensions.
claims.source: General trilateration description (for example the GPS.gov overview of how GPS works; cited from memory, not re-fetched). Real GPS uses four satellites and solves for a clock error; the lesson makes no accuracy claim and says only 'the same idea'.

claims.text: Equal Earth map, zoomed on Europe; sphere model for the distances.
claims.source: Equal Earth projection (Savric, Patterson & Jenny 2018); the map is clipped to Europe by scaling the projection. Rings are drawn with d3-geo geoCircle on a sphere of R = 6,371.0088 km.

recall.question: You know you are 500 km from one city and 600 km from another. How many places usually fit?
options: Two, where the two circles cross
Infinitely many along a straight line
recall.why: Each distance is a circle around its city; two circles meet in two points, and a third distance is needed to choose between them.
